pages.task: 2 L of gas at 3 bar absolute is pushed into 1 L. Its temperature stays the same. What is its absolute pressure now?
pages.why: With the temperature held, pressure × volume stays the same. It starts at 3 × 2 = 6. In 1 L that needs 6 bar absolute. Half the space gives twice the push.

pages.name: Two readings
pages.text: [[Pressure]] is force ÷ area, in pascals, like stress. 1 bar is 100 kPa, about the air's push. A gauge open to the air reads zero. So it reads how far the gas is above the air. That is [[gauge pressure]]. Add the air's 1 bar for [[absolute pressure]], counted from true zero. The temperature is held. Pushed from 3 L to 1.5 L, the absolute pressure doubles, from 2 bar to 4 bar. That is [[Boyle's law]]. The gauge goes from 1 bar to 3, not 2.

pages.name: Half the space
pages.task: A gauge reads 3 bar. The gas is squeezed into half its space, at the same temperature. What does the gauge read now?
pages.why: A gauge reading 3 bar means the gas pushes with 4 bar absolute. Half the space doubles that to 8 bar absolute. The gauge leaves out the air's 1 bar, so it reads 7 bar.

pages.name: A straight line
pages.text: The piston is locked now, so the volume is held. As the gas warms, its pressure climbs in a straight line. Carried on, the line reaches zero pressure at about −273 °C. That is [[absolute zero]], where the kelvin scale starts: K = °C + 273. Pressure is in proportion to kelvin. That is the [[pressure law]]. 27 °C to 127 °C is almost five times the Celsius figure. But 300 K to 400 K is only a third more, so 2 bar becomes about 2.67.

pages.name: Locked and warmed
pages.task: A locked cylinder holds gas at 2 bar absolute and 20 °C. It warms to 40 °C. What is its absolute pressure now?
pages.why: In kelvin, 20 °C is 293 K and 40 °C is 313 K. That is only about 7% warmer. So the pressure rises about 7%: 2 × 313 ÷ 293, about 2.1 bar absolute.

pages.name: A floating piston
pages.text: Now the piston floats under a steady load. The load holds the pressure at 2 bar absolute. As the gas warms from 27 °C to 127 °C, the pressure stays put. In kelvin that is 300 K to 400 K, a third more. So the gas pushes the piston up instead. Its 3 L grows to 4 L, a third more, in step with the kelvin temperature. That is [[Charles's law]].

pages.name: Heating, floating
pages.task: The piston floats under a steady load. The gas warms from 300 K to 450 K. What happens?
pages.answer: The pressure stays the same, and the volume grows by half
pages.why: The load sets the pressure, so it stays at 2 bar absolute. The gas grows instead. 450 ÷ 300 is half as much again, so 3 L becomes 4.5 L.

pages.name: pV ÷ T
pages.text: Pressure is in proportion to kelvin, and in inverse proportion to volume. So for the same trapped gas, pressure × volume ÷ kelvin temperature stays the same, even when all three change. That is [[pV ÷ T]]. In absolute pressure and kelvin it holds at 0.020, whatever changes. Switched to gauge pressure, it drifts, in red. In °C it drifts too. Both count from the wrong zero.

pages.task: Gas at 1 bar absolute fills 6 L at 27 °C. It is pushed into 2 L and heated to 127 °C. What is its absolute pressure now?
pages.why: Work in absolute units. A third of the space triples the pressure: 1 × 6 ÷ 2 = 3 bar. Then 300 K to 400 K adds a third: 3 × 400 ÷ 300 = 4 bar absolute.

pages.name: The air receiver
pages.text: An [[air receiver]] stores air the compressor has already made. It cannot make more. Its compressor cuts out at 8 bar gauge and cuts in at 6. That is 9 and 7 bar absolute. Only the air in that band is used between starts. Let out at 1 bar, this 500 L receiver's air fills 4,500 L at cut-out and 3,500 L at cut-in. So the band gives 1,000 L. At 250 L a minute, that lasts 4 minutes. A receiver twice the size lasts twice as long.

pages.name: Air gone
pages.task: A receiver falls from 8 to 6 bar gauge at a steady temperature. What share of its air has gone?
pages.why: Take the 500 L receiver from before. At 9 bar absolute its air would fill 4,500 L at 1 bar. At 7 bar it fills 3,500 L. So 1,000 of the 4,500 L has gone, about 22%. Any size gives the same share: 2 of 9 bar absolute.
